learn.hook: Gold so thin you can see light through it, and a metal that melts in your palm — metals are full of surprises!
points: Metals are usually lustrous, hard, malleable (beaten into sheets), ductile (drawn into wires), sonorous and good conductors of heat and electricity. Silver and copper are the best conductors.
Exceptions: mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature; sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife; gallium and caesium melt on your palm.

Non-metals are usually dull, brittle and poor conductors; they are solids or gases, but bromine is a liquid. Iodine is lustrous, graphite conducts electricity and diamond is the hardest natural substance.
Metals form basic oxides (e.g. MgO), while non-metals form acidic oxides (e.g. SO₂, CO₂). Aluminium oxide and zinc oxide are amphoteric — they react with both acids and bases.
Very reactive metals like sodium and potassium catch fire in air, so they are stored under kerosene. Silver and gold do not react with oxygen even at high temperature.

example.q: Think it through: a shiny grey solid conducts electricity, but it is brittle and breaks when hammered. Is it a metal?
steps: Conducting electricity alone is not enough — graphite (a non-metal) conducts too.
Metals are malleable; they flatten instead of shattering.
Iodine and graphite show that some non-metals can be lustrous or conducting.
example.answer: Probably not: being brittle points to a non-metal (like graphite), even though it conducts.

learn.reallife: Copper wires carry electricity in your home, aluminium foil wraps your rotis, and copper-bottom vessels heat dal evenly — all thanks to metallic properties.

games.title: Metal myths and facts
items: All metals are solids at room temperature.
Mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature.
Sodium and potassium are stored under kerosene.
They react so vigorously with air and moisture that they can catch fire.
Aluminium oxide reacts with both acids and bases.
It is an amphoteric oxide, like zinc oxide.
Lead and mercury are among the best conductors of heat.
They are comparatively poor conductors of heat; silver and copper are the best.
Gold and silver are the most malleable metals.
They can be beaten into extremely thin sheets.
Sulphur dioxide dissolves in water to give an acidic solution.
Non-metal oxides are generally acidic; SO₂ forms sulphurous acid.

quiz.q: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
quiz.explain: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Gallium melts only when warmed, as on a palm.
quiz.mistake: Confuses low melting point with being liquid at room temperature

quiz.q: Which non-metal is a good conductor of electricity?
quiz.explain: Graphite, a form of carbon, conducts electricity — an exception among non-metals.
quiz.mistake: Thinks lustrous iodine must conduct

quiz.q: Which oxide is amphoteric?
quiz.explain: Zinc oxide (like aluminium oxide) reacts with both acids and bases to form salt and water.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every metal oxide is only basic

quiz.q: Why are electric cooking pans often given handles of plastic or wood?
options: Plastic and wood are good conductors of heat
They help the pan heat faster
Plastic and wood are poor conductors of heat, so the handle stays cool
quiz.explain: The metal body conducts heat to the food, while the poorly conducting handle protects your hand.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up conductor and insulator

quiz.q: The property that allows metals to be drawn into thin wires is called —
quiz.explain: Ductility is being drawn into wires; malleability is being beaten into sheets.
quiz.mistake: Swaps malleability and ductility

quiz.q: A metal that can be cut with a knife is —
quiz.explain: Sodium and potassium are soft metals that can be cut with a knife.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all metals are hard

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a property of most non-metals?
options: They are poor conductors of electricity
They are brittle in solid form
quiz.explain: Sonority (ringing sound when struck) is a property of metals, which is why temple bells are made of metal.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up metallic and non-metallic properties

quiz.q: Which is the hardest natural substance known?
quiz.explain: Diamond, a form of carbon (a non-metal), is the hardest natural substance and has a very high melting point.
quiz.mistake: Assumes metals are always harder than non-metals

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Bells ring, wires bend, foils flatten... but graphite conducts too! How do I tell a metal from a non-metal?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Shiny, bendy, wire-making, conducting — metal! And graphite is a rare non-metal exception.
teach.nudge: Good! Can you add what happens when a metal is beaten or stretched?

learn.hook: Metals compete like players in a kabaddi match — the stronger one always pulls the other out!
points: Reactivity series (most to least reactive): K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.
With water: Na and K react violently with cold water; Ca reacts less violently; Mg reacts with hot water; Al, Zn and Fe react only with steam; Pb, Cu, Ag and Au do not react.

Metals above hydrogen give hydrogen gas with dilute HCl. Nitric acid is an oxidising agent, so it usually does not give hydrogen (except Mg and Mn with very dilute HNO₃). Aqua regia (3 parts conc. HCl : 1 part conc. HNO₃) dissolves even gold.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.

Metals lose electrons and non-metals gain them, forming ionic compounds such as NaCl (Na: 2,8,1 → Na⁺; Cl: 2,8,7 → Cl⁻). Ionic compounds are hard, brittle solids with high melting points, dissolve in water but not in kerosene, and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved, not as solids.

example.q: Think it through: why do calcium pieces start floating in water a little while after being dropped in?
steps: Calcium reacts with water: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂.
Bubbles of hydrogen gas stick to the surface of the metal.
The bubbles make the calcium buoyant.
example.answer: Hydrogen bubbles stick to the calcium and make it float.

learn.reallife: Copper and silver are used for jewellery and coins partly because they are low in the reactivity series and stay unreacted for a long time.

items.q: Metal that reacts with hot water but not cold?
Gas given off when zinc meets dilute HCl?
Aqua regia dissolves this yellow metal?
Ion formed when Cl gains one electron?
Electrons in the outer shell of sodium?
Acid mixed with HNO₃ to make aqua regia?

quiz.q: Which metal reacts violently with cold water?
quiz.explain: Potassium is at the top of the series and reacts so vigorously with cold water that the hydrogen catches fire.
quiz.mistake: Thinks common metals like iron react quickly with water

quiz.q: An iron nail is dipped in zinc sulphate solution. What happens?
options: No reaction, because zinc is more reactive than iron
quiz.explain: Only a more reactive metal can displace a less reactive one. Zinc is above iron, so iron cannot push it out.
quiz.mistake: Assumes any metal will displace any other

quiz.q: What is the ratio of concentrated HCl to concentrated HNO₃ in aqua regia?
quiz.explain: Aqua regia is freshly mixed 3 parts concentrated hydrochloric acid to 1 part concentrated nitric acid.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the ratio

quiz.q: Why is hydrogen usually NOT evolved when a metal reacts with nitric acid?
options: Metals do not react with nitric acid
Nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent and oxidises the hydrogen to water
quiz.explain: HNO₃ oxidises the hydrogen formed into water and itself is reduced to nitrogen oxides.
quiz.mistake: Thinks nitric acid does not contain hydrogen

quiz.q: What is the electronic configuration of the sodium ion, Na⁺?
quiz.explain: Sodium (2, 8, 1) loses its single outer electron to form Na⁺ with a stable 2, 8 arrangement.
quiz.mistake: Writes the configuration of the neutral atom

quiz.q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but its solution in water does. Why?
options: The solid has no ions at all
In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions; in solution they can move
Sodium chloride turns into a metal in water
quiz.explain: Ions are present in the solid but locked in place by strong attraction. Dissolving lets them move and carry charge.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ions form only when the salt dissolves

quiz.q: Which metal reacts with steam but NOT with cold or hot water?
quiz.explain: Iron reacts with steam: 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂. Silver does not react even with steam.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all metals react with water in the same way

quiz.q: Ionic compounds generally dissolve in —
quiz.explain: Ionic compounds are soluble in water but generally insoluble in kerosene and petrol.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ionic compounds behave like oils

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why can zinc steal copper's place in copper sulphate, but copper can't steal zinc's? What is this reactivity series?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Zinc is higher in the reactivity series, so it displaces copper. Copper is too weak to fight back!
teach.nudge: Good! Which one is more reactive — zinc or copper? That's the key.

topics.title: Extraction of metals, corrosion and alloys

learn.hook: Gold lies almost pure in the ground, but sodium hides inside salt — how reactive a metal is decides how we dig it out!
points: Minerals are natural compounds of metals; an ore is a mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably. Unwanted earthy impurities are called gangue.

Low reactivity metals (Hg, Cu) are obtained by heating their ores in air, e.g. cinnabar (HgS) gives mercury. Middle metals (Zn, Fe, Pb): sulphide ores are roasted (heated strongly in excess air) and carbonate ores calcined (heated in limited air) to get oxides, which are reduced with carbon.

The thermit reaction Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Fe + Al₂O₃ releases so much heat that the iron forms molten, so it is used to join railway tracks. Highly reactive metals (Na, Mg, Ca, Al) are extracted by electrolysis of their molten compounds.

Electrolytic refining: impure metal is the anode, a thin strip of pure metal is the cathode, and a salt solution of the metal is the electrolyte. Pure metal collects on the cathode; insoluble impurities settle as anode mud.

Corrosion: silver turns black (silver sulphide), copper turns green (basic copper carbonate) and iron rusts. It is prevented by painting, oiling, greasing, galvanising (zinc coating), chrome plating, anodising and making alloys such as stainless steel (iron + nickel + chromium), brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn) and solder (Pb + Sn).

example.q: Think it through: why is a galvanised iron bucket protected from rusting even if its zinc coating gets scratched?
steps: Zinc is more reactive than iron.
Zinc corrodes in place of iron, so the exposed iron is still protected.
example.answer: Zinc, being more reactive, reacts first and continues to protect the iron.

learn.reallife: The famous iron pillar near the Qutub Minar in Delhi has stood for centuries without rusting — a tribute to the skill of ancient Indian iron workers. Gold jewellery is usually 22 carat: 22 parts gold mixed with 2 parts copper or silver to make it harder.

Remove gangue (enrichment)

games.title: Match the alloy to its metals

quiz.q: What is gangue?
options: The pure metal obtained from an ore
Earthy impurities such as soil and sand in an ore
quiz.explain: Ores dug from the earth carry unwanted rock, soil and sand, called gangue, which must be removed first.
quiz.mistake: Confuses gangue with the ore itself

quiz.q: Heating a carbonate ore strongly in limited air is called —
quiz.explain: Calcination converts carbonate ores to oxides, e.g. ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂. Roasting is for sulphide ores in excess air.
quiz.mistake: Swaps roasting and calcination

quiz.q: Why can't sodium be obtained by heating its oxide with carbon?
options: Carbon is more reactive than everything
Sodium has more attraction for oxygen than carbon has
Sodium is found free in nature
quiz.explain: Sodium is very high in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot remove oxygen from it. Electrolysis of molten sodium chloride is used.
quiz.mistake: Thinks carbon can reduce every metal oxide

quiz.q: In electrolytic refining of copper, the cathode is —
options: A thin strip of pure copper
quiz.explain: Pure copper from the solution deposits on the thin pure copper cathode; the impure copper is the anode.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the anode and cathode

quiz.q: Which reaction is used to join broken railway tracks?
quiz.explain: The thermit reaction gives so much heat that iron forms in the molten state and fills the gap.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the heat of the thermit reaction to its use

quiz.q: Silver ornaments turn black over time because they react with —
quiz.explain: Silver reacts with sulphur compounds in air to form a black coating of silver sulphide.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the black layer is silver oxide or rust

quiz.q: Galvanisation means coating iron or steel with —
quiz.explain: A thin zinc layer protects iron from rusting even if scratched.
quiz.mistake: Confuses galvanising with chrome plating or tinning

quiz.q: Why is solder used to join electrical wires?
options: It has a high melting point
It has a low melting point
quiz.explain: Solder (lead + tin) melts at a low temperature, so it can be melted easily to join wires. Alloys often melt at lower temperatures than their pure metals.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a joining metal should be hard to melt

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does Papa's iron gate get painted every year? What is rusting and how do we stop it?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Air and water make iron rust, so paint or zinc keeps them away. Smart gate!
teach.nudge: Nearly! What two things from the surroundings cause iron to rust?
